messages.subject: Unidimensional longitudinal model in MIRT with common itens
messages.subject_clean: Unidimensional longitudinal model in MIRT with common itens
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I am trying to write a unidimensional longitudinal model in MIRT like below. Same group of people being evaluated at different times using different item sets with a small subset of common items for scale equalization.

In my sample code I have 60 items, 30 at each moment with items 21:30 and 31:40 being the same between moments. I wrote the model like below but I keep getting a message about constraining fixed parameters. I know how to model such situation using multigroup but I would like to take the covariance between the latent variables of the two moments into account. Am I missing something?

> model_U <- '
> F1=1-30
> F2=31-60
> CONSTRAIN =(21,31,a1),(22,32,a1),(23,33,a1),(24,34,a1),(25,35,a1),(26,36,a1),(27,37,a1),(28,38,a1),(29,39,a1),(30,40,a1)
> CONSTRAIN =(21,31,d), (22,32,d), (23,33,d),(24,34,d),(25,35,d),(26,36,d),(27,37,d),(28,38,d),(29,39,d),(30,40,d)
> COV = F1*F2
> '
> mod <-mirt(data=U[,c(1:60)],itemtype = "2PL",model=model_U)
>
> Erro: Constraint applied to fixed parameter(s) 151 156 161 166 171 176 181 186 191 196  but should only be applied to estimated parameters. Please fix!
>
Looking forward to hearing from you,

Hugo

Here is where I get stuck - although I have specified "printSE = T", I get only the and b parameter estimates but not their SE:

messages.subject: createItem Function
messages.subject_clean: createItem Function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Everyone,

I'm trying to fit a complementary log log version of the 2PL model (not sure if this has a name in the IRT literature). I've been using the createItem function to do so like so:

name <- 'cloglog'
par <- c(a = .5, b = 2)
est <- c(TRUE, TRUE)
P.cloglog <- function(par, Theta, ncat){
  a <- par[1]
  b <- par[2]
  P1 <- 1 - exp(-exp(a*(Theta - b)))
  cbind(1 - P1, P1)
}
clog <- createItem(name, par=par, est=est, P=P.cloglog)
m2 <- mirt(grammar_short, 1, "cloglog", customItems=list(cloglog=clog))

With some sets of starting values, the model converges immediately and I get a warning. With other starting values, the model converges after 2 or 3 iterations, but the fit is really poor. I've tried reducing the tolerance but that doesn't change anything. I don't have any problems when I use MIRT's in-built model types with this data set. I'm assuming there's an error with the code above somewhere, but can't find it. Does anybody see anything?

thanks!
Seamus

Dear All,
Is there a (relatively) easy way to change the probability of correct response in the customNextItem-Function? For instance, due to motivational considerations, you want to make the CAT a bit easier and increase the probability of correct response to .65 when selecting the (next) items. Is this possible? Bergstrom et al. (1992) describe such an approach, but I am unsure how to implement this.

Thanks a ton!
Best wishes
Christoph

messages.subject_clean: Multidimensional between-item CAT (MCAT)
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Aug 24, 2021 at 5:06 AM strate <nick.str...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> I'm trying to adapt/simulate a personality test (14 distinct, but intercorrelated dimensions from 210 polytomous items) as a CAT from real data in 3 steps. My goal is to study the efficiency of CAT in comparison to linear testing for this questionnaire.
>
> First I interpreted each dimension as an unidimensional factor, separated the items into 14 different datasets, fitted 14 unidimensional GRM-models and administered 14 independent UCATs. Up to this point, that worked well: The UCATs need only around 50% of the items in average.
>
> Now second I want to run an MCAT with all 14 dimensions and the compete dataset, but uncorrelated, so as to compare the results to step 1. I fitted a mirt-model like this:
>
> model <- 'F1 =  7, 22, 37, 53, 69, 85, 100, 115, 130, 144, 159, 172, 196, 204
>
>                  F2 =  8, 23, 38, 54, 70, 86, 101, 116, 131, 145, 173, 186
>
>                  F3 =  9, 24, 39, 55, 71, 87, 102, 117, 132, 146, 160, 174, 187, 197, 205
>
>                  F4 =  11, 26, 41, 57, 73, 89, 104, 119, 134, 148, 162, 176, 188, 206
>
>                  F5 =  12, 27, 42, 58, 74, 90, 105, 120, 135, 149, 163, 177, 189, 198
>
>                  F6 =  13, 28, 43, 59, 75, 91, 106, 121, 136, 150, 164, 178, 190, 199
>
>                  F7 =  14, 29, 44, 60, 76, 92, 107, 122, 151, 165, 179, 191
>
>                  F8 =  2, 16, 31, 46, 62, 78, 94, 109, 124, 138, 153, 167, 181, 192, 201, 208
>
>                  F9=  1, 15, 30, 45, 61, 77, 93, 108, 123, 137, 152, 166, 180, 200, 207
>
>                  F10 =  3, 17, 32, 47, 63, 79, 95, 110, 125, 139, 154, 168, 182
>
>                  F11 =  10, 25, 40, 56, 72, 88, 103, 118, 133, 147, 161, 175
>
>                  F12 =  4, 18, 33, 48, 64, 80, 96, 111, 126, 140, 155, 169, 183, 193, 202, 209
>
>                  F13 =  5, 19, 34, 49, 65, 81, 97, 112, 127, 141, 156, 170, 184
>
>                  F14 =  6, 20, 35, 50, 66, 82, 98, 113, 128, 142, 157, 171, 185, 194, 203, 210'
>
>
> Generated the mirt-model like:
>
> mirt.model <- mirt(data, model = model, 'graded', cl = cl, method = "MHRM")
>
>
> And ran the MCAT like this:
>
> cat.design <- list(min_items = 5, min_SEM = 0.35, delta_thetas = 0.05) #Same as in UCATs
>
> result <- mirtCAT(mo = mirt.model, local_pattern = data.pattern, start_item = 'Drule', criteria = 'Drule', design = cat.design)
>
>
> Yet, the thetas of the MCAT for each factor are not remotely comparable to the results of the different UCATs from step 1. There are only around 20 items from 210 selected, SE is quite high (NOT around .35 as wanted). I would have guessed the MCAT would work quite similar to a bunch of UCATs when the factors are treated as uncorrelated. Can you spot my mistake? Is there a way to tell mirtCAT to use the termination criteria (like min_item = 5) for each factor separately?

How close were the multidimensional item parameters to the unidimensional ones that you calibrated? The MIRT models are not really free to estimate as the integrals have to be evaluated using stochastic estimation. Plus, the selection criteria is slightly different (determinant rule is trying to pick items that minimize the overall volume of the measurement uncertainty, rather than a single unidimensional slice).

Regarding your follow-up questions, mirtCAT doesn't support termination based on single factor criteria like min_items for each dimension, but you could certainly do this if you use some of the customization functions that you can define yourself.

>
>
> Then for step 3, I want to repeat the MCAT but with respect to the intercorrelations of the dimensions. As those are quite highly correlated, I expect an even better efficiency in comparison to step 1 and 2. How can I include the intercorrelations into my model? I assume something like 'COV = F1*F2*...*F14' in the model definition - is that correct? Is there a possibility to tell mirt specific correlations/covarinces (for example as a cov-matrix)?

Yes, that would work to define all correlation parameters.

messages.subject: Re: SE for a and b parameters for the 2-parameter Logistic Model on 3 binary items
messages.subject_clean: SE for a and b parameters for the 2-parameter Logistic Model on 3 binary items
messages.body_plain:
Standard errors are not computed by default due to the use of the EM algorithm default; hence, you need to pass mirt(..., SE = TRUE).

X2* doesn't follow the usual df comparison in the large sample sense, and instead uses a bootstrapping methodology based on resampling and permutations.

Regarding the bootstrap, I believe this is only supported for the slope-intercept parameterizations. It's possible to pass a secondary function to boot.mirt(), but this is currently not supported. I'll consider adding this to the next version of the package. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: mirt - second order model
messages.subject_clean: mirt - second order model
messages.body_plain:
I'm not 100% sure what is being asked here, but in case this is just about how to obtain the associated parameters for a higher-order model after having fit a testlet model via bfactor() the result is reasonably straightforward. For the higher-order model the form is

P(y|θ,ψ) = ∑ as θs + d

where the θs terms are models according to the general factor θs = βs θg + ϵ. However, rather than fitting this model the testlet response model can be fit instead to impose the proportionality constraints, and then back-transformed when the model converges. Below is an example of this from the manual:

##########
library(mirt)

#simulate data
set.seed(1234)
a <- matrix(0, 12, 4)
a[,1] <- rlnorm(12, .2, .3)
ind <- 1
for(i in 1:3){
   a[ind:(ind+3),i+1] <- a[ind:(ind+3),1]
   ind <- ind+4
}
print(a)
d <- rnorm(12, 0, .5)
sigma <- diag(c(1, .5, 1, .5))
dataset <- simdata(a,d,2000,itemtype=rep('2PL', 12),sigma=sigma)

# estimate by applying constraints and freeing the latent variances
specific <- c(rep(1,4),rep(2,4), rep(3,4))
model <- "G = 1-12
          CONSTRAIN = (1, a1, a2), (2, a1, a2), (3, a1, a2), (4, a1, a2),
            (5, a1, a3), (6, a1, a3), (7, a1, a3), (8, a1, a3),
            (9, a1, a4), (10, a1, a4), (11, a1, a4), (12, a1, a4)
          COV = S1*S1, S2*S2, S3*S3"

simmod <- bfactor(dataset, specific, model)
coef(simmod, simplify=TRUE)
####

>From this output the loadings on either the general of specific factor correspond to the same loadings as in the higher-order model (as they're constrained to be equal), while the β coefficients are obtained by way of the transformation 1/√{VAR(θs)). Using the above output, just use

###
cov <- coef(simmod, simplify=TRUE)$cov
betas <- 1 / sqrt(diag(cov)[-1L])
betas
###

HTH.

Phil
